name: Nokuku
confidence_why: No source describes Nokuku word stress: Ray 1926 and Gordon 1889 say nothing about accent, and Clark 2009 states that no published phonology of Nokuku exists and uses "stressed (penultimate)" only for the historical Proto-North-Central-Vanuatu stress position, before the final-vowel loss that leaves those vowels word-final in modern Nokuku.
catalog_citation: Clark, Ross. 2009. Leo Tuai: A comparative lexical study of North and Central Vanuatu languages. Pacific Linguistics 603. Canberra: ANU (open access, hdl.handle.net/1885/146751). Sec. 3.4 'Nokuku (Nok)', pp. 25-27; sec. 2.1.3, p. 16. Also checked: Ray, Sidney H. 1926. Grammar of the Nogugu language, in A Comparative Study of the Melanesian Island Languages, 384-401 (Rosetta Project excerpt); Gordon, J. D. 1889. Santo grammar and vocabulary, in D. Macdonald (ed.), South Sea Languages vol. 1: 85-134.
catalog_locator: Clark 2009 p. 25 'Phonemes and spelling'; p. 27 'Changes: Vowels'; p. 16 sec. 2.1.3. Ray 1926 p. 384 sec. I 'Alphabet' §§1-2.
catalog_quote: No published description of Nokuku phonology exists, but my own investigation together with the sources listed suggests the following phonemic inventory. [p.25] ... Post-consonantal final vowels are lost in present day Nokuku, but are present in the early records by Gordon and McKenzie. ... Stressed (penultimate) vowels are generally unchanged except that *a > ɔ before a final high vowel: *damu > ʔɔm ‘yam’, *avi > ɔv ‘fire’. Pre-stress (antepenultimate) *a is assimilated to a following high vowel: to e when the following vowel is i, and to o when the following vowel is u: kani-a > kenia ‘eat (vt)’, *ʔavua > ovua ‘turtle’, *natu-na > notuna ‘his/her child’. ... Examples suggest that the dissimilation of *a > e is the earliest of these changes, followed by the shift of stressed *a to ɔ and then final vowel deletion. Thus *baravu > *beravu > *berɔvu > perɔw ‘long’, *vatali > *vetali > *vetɔli > vetɔl ‘banana’. [p.27] ... Word stress in PNCV was most likely on the penultimate vowel. This is its position in almost all daughter languages for which phonological descriptions exist, where the historic final syllable is intact. [p.16]
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: At face value: the stressed vowel is the (historically) penultimate one, i.e. the PNCV penult, and antepenultimate vowels are pre-stress. But this is a diachronic statement about PNCV > Nokuku vowel changes, not a synchronic placement rule: Clark says explicitly that no published Nokuku phonology exists and gives no stress line in the Nokuku phoneme block (he does for Mota, Raga, Tamambo, etc.). Since present-day Nokuku has lost post-consonantal final vowels (p.27), the historically penultimate stressed vowel is now often the final syllable (ʔɔm, ɔv, perɔw, vetɔl), so the synchronic position is undetermined from this source.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress placement; the vowel changes are described as 'generally' holding, with dissimilation and labial conditioning exceptions for the vowel qualities.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, cited forms only (cognate reflexes drawn from Mackenzie's 1906/1918 translations, Ray 1926, Gordon 1889, Tryon 1976 and Clark's own 2005-2007 field notes). Family-level context, p.16: 'Word stress in PNCV was most likely on the penultimate vowel. This is its position in almost all daughter languages for which phonological descriptions exist, where the historic final syllable is intact.'
new_statements.identity_note: Nokuku = Nogugu (Ray 1926, Mackenzie's orthography) = Tanokuk (local name used by Taman, Taman & Rangelov 2025, c. 849 L1 speakers, Poaru to Ravlepa) = 'Santo' of Gordon in Macdonald 1889 (with 'Walua'/Valpei dialect forms). Lynch & Crowley 2001 (sec. 3.3.7) treat it as a dialect of a 'Cape Cumberland' language together with Valpei (valp1237), Tasmate (tasm1246), Vunapu (vuna1239) and Piamatsina (piam1242); Glottolog and Clark 2009 keep noku1237 as a separate language, closest to Valpei. All sources examined concern this same variety.
